description: I’m Mansoor, a senior Android developer at PITB in Pakistan with an M.Phil in CS. I build mobile apps in Kotlin and Jetpack Compose and like putting AI models on phones. I’ve built and mentored at hackathons, so I’ll help get a working demo done and help anyone who’s new. Pak Angels is looking for a data/GIS person (NASA Earthdata), a UI/UX designer, a backend developer, and someone who can handle the story and demo video. Beginners welcome. Message me with what you’re good at.
summary:
We built Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer, a browser game where kids run a Moon or Mars outpost. Each day, they decide how to spend power, materials, and crew time. Switching off the greenhouse saves power but stops food production. A daily report shows what happened and why, so players can see how today’s choices affect tomorrow’s mission.

How does it address the challenge?

The first mission starts with power, air, and radiation. Food and water come later, so even a 7-year-old can learn one step at a time. Solar storms use real events from NASA’s DONKI database and show each flare’s date and size. NASA’s Open Science Data Repository informs the science notes, and Moon and Mars radiation data help shape each site. Data is labeled live, saved, or sample. The “Today’s Sun” mission uses recent space weather to keep missions changing. Mission Control replies right away on the Moon, while the game makes Mars crews wait a turn to show why they need to make decisions on their own.

Why is it important?

Kids can try a plan, see why it failed, and make a better one. That gives them a hands-on way to think like mission planners. The game runs in a browser without a download or account, so classrooms and families can play right away.
details:
What exactly does it do?

It’s a turn-based game where one turn is one day at a small Moon or Mars outpost. A kid looks after three astronauts and decides how to spend limited crew time and materials. They can build solar panels, batteries, a small nuclear reactor called Kilopower, radiation shielding, a greenhouse, and a better water and air recycler. They can also change settings like life support mode and greenhouse level. At the end of each day, a short report explains what happened in plain words, for example “The sun gave 8 power units. The base used 9.” There are three missions plus a “Today’s Sun” mission. Each ends with a report that says why the crew made it or didn’t, and a tip for next time.

How does it work?

All the rules live in a simulation that runs once per day. It works out how much power the panels make, how much each system uses, and what gets switched off if power runs short. Then it updates oxygen, water, food, radiation, and each astronaut’s health and morale. Solar storms come from real NASA flare records, scaled to the game, and the player has to choose between spending stored power on a storm shelter or hiding in the habitat and losing a day’s work. The Ask Mission Control button gives a hint from Earth, instantly on the Moon and a day later on Mars. The app checks NASA’s DONKI service for recent space weather. If it can’t reach it, it uses a saved snapshot and labels it clearly.

What are the benefits?

Kids learn by seeing cause and effect, not by reading facts. Because every choice has a cost, there is no “safe” button to spam. Failing is gentle: the mission ends as “aborted,” with an explanation and an instant retry. It works offline, needs no account, and teachers get a short summary of what the student met and decided.

What do you hope to achieve?

We want a kid to walk away knowing one real thing: that astronauts can’t have everything at once, and that planning ahead is what keeps a crew safe. We also want it to be something a classroom can actually use.

Tools and technology

  • Flutter and Dart for the app, with a web build for browsers and an Android build
  • Riverpod for state, shared_preferences for saving progress, and audioplayers for sound
  • Custom drawing in Flutter for the outpost scene and charts, with sound effects generated by a script
  • NASA DONKI API for solar flares and particle events, plus NASA OSDR research and Artemis and Mars surface mission data
  • flutter_test for tests and a small Dart script that plays the game with simple bots to balance difficulty
  • Claude for planning, writing the specs, and helping write code.
  • No special hardware. Tested on Android Phone and Chrome Browser.
